Adding an AI Tool to Google Earth Shook Our Trust in Maps That Has Been Centuries in the Making

2026-08-06 James Cheshire, The Conversation Google Earth, generative AI, trust in maps, cartographic history, Mountains of Kong, satellite imagery, map copyright, AI ethics
Read the source article

Quick summary

A professor of cartography traces how Google's addition of generative AI to Google Earth—enabling convincing but fictional satellite images—challenges centuries of trust placed in mapmaking technology, from ancient surveying instruments to modern satellites.

Key takeaways

  • Google added generative AI to Google Earth, making it possible to create convincing but fictional satellite images, which some users quickly used to create disturbing content like bombed suburbs
  • The article draws a historical parallel with the mythical "Mountains of Kong" that appeared on African maps for over a century after explorer Mungo Park's 1790s expedition, showing how map errors persist
  • A 1785 copyright case involving London map publishers established precedent cited in modern AI copyright defenses: works can build on earlier material if they're not "servile imitations"
  • Trust in mapmaking technology has been a constant from the ancient Greek dioptra to modern satellites, but generative AI now threatens that trust
  • The article argues that maps have a lasting impact on how we see and understand the world, and that AI-generated map content requires careful consideration of trust and verification
